explanations: terra: A party hears God's word, understands it, and then knowingly distorts it, explicitly separating physical hearing, understanding, and obedient fidelity.
terra: The answer “we hear and disobey” severs audition from obedience, directly marking the failed sense of سماع against the section's fuller definition.
terra: Here اللَّغْوِ in oaths is unintentional or ineffective speech for which God does not take people to account; this different legal sense marks a semantic boundary from 88:11's ugly utterance.

luna: The believers answer revelation with “we hear and obey,” showing the section's obedience-sense of سماع in response to the scripture. | terra: The believers answer revelation with سَمِعْنَا وَأَطَعْنَا, making hearing explicitly culminate in obedience as the section's dictionary sense requires.
terra: After the invitation to submit, the Prophet is told that if they turn away his duty is only conveyance, matching the limited commission at 88:21–22.

luna: Mary's guardianship is called news of the unseen revealed to the Prophet though he was not present; the ayah grounds the section's revelation route for a report. | terra: Mary's story is unseen news revealed to the Prophet, who was not present at the casting of lots; the absent event reaches him as report.

luna: The believers say they heard a caller summoning them to faith and then believed, carrying the section's path from an arriving utterance to a listener's response. | terra: The believers say they heard a caller calling to faith and consequently believed, an explicit chain from heard proclamation to response.
terra: On Judgment Day those who disobeyed the Messenger wish to be levelled with the earth yet cannot conceal from God حَدِيثًا; the hearer's response has become an inescapable reported fact.

luna: The ayah reports people saying “we hear and disobey” while twisting words; it makes explicit the difference between hearing sound and accepting what is heard. | terra: “سمعنا وعصينا” and the hostile “hear, may you not be heard” corrupt both listening and address, a precise negative boundary around morally sound hearing.

terra: The people are said scarcely to understand any حَدِيثًا, using discourse together with failed comprehension and thereby supporting the section's distinction between hearing words and grasping them.
terra: Whoever obeys the Messenger obeys God, but if people turn away the Prophet has not been sent as their guardian.
terra: The promise that God will gather everyone on Resurrection Day ends by asking who is truer than God in حَدِيثًا; future judgment is guaranteed as truthful report.

luna: When God's verses are denied and mocked, believers must leave until the group takes up another حديث; this sets a boundary around what speech they attend. | terra: When God's signs are heard being denied and mocked, believers must leave until the mockers enter another حديث; the ayah distinguishes revealed speech from corrupt talk surrounding it.
terra: God does not love evil speech voiced publicly except by one wronged, defining an earthly boundary around the kind of ugly utterance Paradise excludes altogether.

luna: The covenant recalls the believers' answer “we hear and obey”; it gives a concrete instance of hearing joined to submission. | terra: The covenantal answer “We hear and obey” connects receiving spoken command with the obedience implicit in سماع.
terra: When they hear what was revealed to the Messenger, their eyes overflow because they recognize truth; heard revelation produces comprehension and bodily response.
terra: God does not take people to account for اللَّغْوِ in oaths but does for deliberate oaths; intention distinguishes this use from the foul or vain speech excluded in Paradise.
terra: If the audience turns away, it must know that the Messenger's duty is only clear delivery, preserving the boundary between speaking and controlling response.
terra: The Messenger's duty is only conveyance while God knows what people disclose and hide, a concise parallel to “you are only a reminder.”

luna: Some listeners have veiled hearts and heaviness in their ears and still disbelieve when signs come; it reverses the garden's receptive hearing. | terra: Some listen to the Prophet while veils cover their hearts and deafness their ears; the ayah separates audible exposure from understanding the report.

luna: After recalling messengers who were denied and remained patient, the ayah says news of the messengers has come to the Prophet, framing earlier stories as support for the present messenger. | terra: Earlier messengers endured denial until God's help came, and some of their news has reached the Prophet; received report steadies the new bearer against rejection.

luna: The ayah says only those who hear respond, then says God will raise the dead; hearing is explicitly tied to response and the coming resurrection. | terra: Only those who truly hear respond, while the dead await resurrection; the ayah turns hearing into spiritual receptivity with final consequences.
terra: When people forget what they were reminded of, ease is opened until sudden seizure, so failure to retain warning turns its audience into a cautionary story.
terra: Although the Prophet's people deny the true message, he says he is not a trustee over them, separating the delivered report from control of its hearers.

luna: When mockers engage God's signs, the Prophet must leave them until they enter another حديث; the boundary protects revelation from degrading discourse. | terra: The Prophet must turn away when people plunge mockingly into God's signs until they enter a different حديث, guarding the setting in which revelation is heard.
terra: The Prophet must leave those who turn religion into play yet remind with the revelation lest a soul be delivered to ruin, joining noncontrol with continued warning.
terra: The revelation is “only a reminder to the worlds,” extending the received message beyond its first addressee to every later audience.
terra: After insights have come from God, seeing or remaining blind belongs to each person, and the Prophet is not their guardian; reception remains the listener's responsibility.
terra: God has not made the Prophet a guardian or trustee over the idolaters, closely paralleling the boundary following 88:21's command to remind.
terra: Humans and jinn are asked whether messengers from among them related God's signs and warned of this Day; they testify against themselves that the report did reach them.
terra: The Book is sent to the Prophet so he may warn with it and as a reminder for believers, combining first reception, proclamation, and remembrance.
luna: The Garden's people say praise to God for guiding them there; this is another specific utterance of gratitude in the quiet setting.
terra: The people of the Heights call “Peace be upon you” to the Garden's people; the greeting is Paradise-directed, though its speakers have not yet entered.
terra: Because they forgot the meeting of the Day and rejected the signs, God “forgets” them that Day; ignored report becomes realized judgment.

luna: The Prophet is told that the towns' news is recounted to him, and that their messengers brought clear proofs which they still rejected; the account makes past peoples cautionary reports. | terra: God tells the Prophet that He relates some news of the ruined towns, making their former response into warning heard by a new audience.
terra: When the wrongdoers forget what they were reminded of, those forbidding evil are saved and the offenders seized, tying remembrance to survival within narrated history.
terra: After signs in creation and the possibility that their term is near, the ayah asks what حديث after this they will believe, treating the revelation as the decisive warning discourse.

luna: When the Qur'an is recited, listeners are told to listen and be silent so that they may receive mercy, a direct command for attentive hearing. | terra: When the Quran is recited, hearers are commanded to listen and be silent; this is voluntary, attentive silence before revelation rather than the frightened hush of 20:108.
terra: When God's signs are recited, believers' faith increases; the arriving words alter their hearers instead of passing through as mere sound.

luna: Believers are commanded to obey God and the Messenger and not turn away while they hear; the ayah makes hearing a call to obedience. | terra: Believers are told to obey God and the Messenger and not turn away while they are hearing, directly joining audition to the obedience included in سماع.

luna: In the battle passage some say “we hear” while in fact not hearing; it exposes the gap between catching words and heeding them that the section's سماع sense allows. | terra: The audience is forbidden to say “we have heard” while they do not truly hear, distinguishing claimed audition from receptive understanding.
terra: Even if God made the unreceptive hear, they would turn away, so sound reception alone is exposed as insufficient without willing obedience.
terra: When the signs are recited, rejecters say they have already heard and dismiss them as tales of the ancients, misclassifying true revelation as disposable old story.
terra: Protection is granted so a seeker may hear كَلَامَ ٱللَّهِ and reach safety; revelation literally reaches a human through the ear before a response is possible.
terra: The question whether news of earlier peoples reached them introduces successive destroyed communities, directly joining transmitted history to the danger of repeating it.

luna: In the Garden their prayer is praise, their greeting is peace, and their final words are praise; the ayah names the good speech replacing harmful talk. | terra: The prayer and greeting of Paradise's people are glorification, peace, and praise, specifying wholesome words heard where vain speech is absent.

luna: Some listen to the Prophet, but the ayah asks whether he can make the deaf hear when they do not reason; it distinguishes sound reaching an ear from understanding it. | terra: Some listen to the Prophet, yet he cannot make the deaf hear when they do not understand; this limits the reminder's power over its audience.

luna: Noah's account is to be recited to the Prophet, and Noah calls his people to reflect on his reminder; it combines a narrated past scene with the messenger's warning. | terra: The Prophet is commanded to recite Noah's news to the people, explicitly turning an old event into spoken warning for a new audience.
terra: Truth has come from the Lord, but each person bears the result of guidance or error and the Prophet is not their trustee.
terra: Amid demands placed on revelation, the Prophet is told he is only a warner while God is trustee over everything, limiting his role to proclamation.
terra: Noah's account is called unseen news revealed to the Prophet, which neither he nor his people knew; revelation is the route by which the report reaches him.
terra: “This is from the news of the towns which We relate to you” explicitly turns surviving and harvested settlements into revealed narrative for the Prophet.
terra: On the coming Day no soul speaks except by God's permission, a direct Judgment scene in which ordinary human speech falls silent.

luna: The Prophet is told that the messengers' accounts are recited to steady him and serve as reminder and admonition for believers, a concrete purpose for received stories. | terra: The news of the messengers is related to steady the Prophet's heart, and in it truth, admonition, and reminder have come to him; received story becomes stabilizing proclamation.
luna: God says He relates the best of stories to the Prophet through this revealed Qur'an; it makes explicit the section's point that a hadith reaches people through revelation as well as hearing.
terra: Joseph says “mention me” to the king, but Satan makes the man forget that mention; one ayah holds ذكر as spoken mention and as the opposite of forgetting.

luna: At Joseph's story's close, the ayah calls it news of the unseen revealed to the Prophet, who was not present at the brothers' plotting; it exemplifies a report arriving by revelation. | terra: Joseph's account is unseen news revealed to the Prophet, who was absent from the scene; the ayah distinguishes transmitted revelation from eyewitness knowledge.
terra: The Prophet asks no payment for the message, which is only a reminder to the worlds; his role is transmission rather than control or gain.

luna: Joseph's and the other messengers' stories contain a lesson, and the Qur'an is not an invented hadith; the ayah joins narrative, report, and the hearer's admonition. | terra: The messengers' stories contain a lesson and are not حَدِيثًا يُفْتَرَىٰ; the ayah marks the transmitted story as truthful revelation meant to instruct its hearer.

luna: Angels greet the patient in the Garden with peace; it is another concrete garden utterance consistent with the section's replacement of laghw by salutations. | terra: Angels enter upon the people of Eden saying “Peace be upon you” for their patience, giving the Garden's audible replacement for ugly speech.

luna: The Prophet's duty is only to convey while the reckoning belongs to God; it defines the messenger's report-bearing role alongside the final accounting in the surah. | terra: The Prophet's duty is only delivery while accounting belongs to God; this anticipates the exact division at 88:21–26 between reminder and divine reckoning.
terra: Moses is told to bring his people from darkness and remind them of God's days, making narrated divine acts an oral warning for a community.
terra: “Has there not come to you the news” of Noah, ʿĀd, and Thamud asks later hearers to receive destroyed peoples as warning, a nonlexical match for the opening and the “become reports” motif.

luna: The people admitted to the gardens have peace as their greeting there, naming the speech that replaces idle or foul talk. | terra: Those admitted to gardens greet one another there with سَلَامٌ, directly populating the section's purified soundscape.
terra: The good word is likened to a firmly rooted, fruit-bearing tree; it supplies a positive moral image for speech where the section excludes the ugly word.
terra: An evil word is like an uprooted tree with no stability, the direct moral opposite of the good word and a concrete image for the ugly speech absent from the Garden.
terra: The righteous are told to enter the gardens in peace and security, placing salām at Paradise's threshold even though the ayah frames it as entry speech rather than reported hearing.

luna: God's command is announced as already having come, followed by a warning not to hasten it; this directly parallels the section's future Day arriving as a report already received. | terra: أَتَىٰ أَمْرُ ٱللَّهِ speaks of God's still-awaited command as already arrived and then forbids haste, the clearest parallel to 88's future Day told as arrived news.
terra: Angels take the good while saying “Peace be upon you; enter the Garden,” so salām is heard at the very threshold of Paradise.
terra: The question whether messengers bear anything beyond clear conveyance repeats the exact limit on the reminder's authority.

luna: God says the reminder was sent down to the Prophet so he can clarify to people what was sent to them; it joins revelation received with the Prophet's reminder-bearing role. | terra: The Reminder is sent down to the Prophet so he may explain to people what was sent to them, a direct relay from first addressee to subsequent hearers.
terra: If they turn away, the Prophet's duty remains only clear conveyance; the hearer's refusal does not enlarge the messenger's authority.
luna: Hearing, sight, and heart will each be questioned, adding accountability to the section's picture of someone who receives a report by ear.

luna: The ayah describes veils over hearts and heaviness in ears when the Qur'an is recited, followed by turning away; it depicts blocked reception of the reminder. | terra: Veils over hearts and heaviness in ears prevent understanding during Quranic recitation, so listeners turn away when God's oneness is mentioned.
terra: God knows how opponents listen to the Prophet and what they say in private counsel, bringing public hearing and concealed hostile speech into one scene.
terra: On the Day God calls, people respond with praise and realize how briefly they remained, showing the final call producing unavoidable response.
terra: The Prophet must tell God's servants to say what is best because Satan sows discord through speech, an earthly discipline corresponding to Paradise's purified words.
terra: God knows the audience best and has not sent the Prophet as their trustee, limiting the human speaker while leaving judgment to God.
terra: When the Quran is recited, those given prior knowledge fall on their faces in prostration, an embodied answer to the arriving word that leads into 17:109's khushūʿ.

luna: After 17:107-108 describe learned listeners hearing Qur'an and prostrating, this ayah says they weep and grow in humility, showing a response to recited revelation. | terra: Those given knowledge fall on their faces weeping as recitation increases their خُشُوعًا, connecting revealed words with the bodily humility whose acoustic form the section hears.
terra: The Prophet nearly consumes himself with grief if people do not believe “this حديث”; against that burden, 88:21 defines his role as giving the reminder.
terra: God says He relates the Companions' news to the Prophet in truth, another revealed story that reaches one addressee for proclamation.
terra: “Remember your Lord when you forget” states exactly the dictionary opposition the section uses to explain the reminder's work in its listener.

luna: The ayah describes someone reminded of the Lord's signs who turns away, forgets, and has deafness in the ears; it is a specific failure to receive the reminder the section traces. | terra: The one reminded of God's signs turns away and forgets his own deeds while deafness covers his ears, bringing reminder, forgetting, and failed hearing together.
luna: Asked about Dhul-Qarnayn, the Prophet is told to recite a remembrance of him, turning a question into a spoken account as in the section's opening frame.
terra: Those whose eyes were veiled from God's reminder could not bear to hear, the negative union of blocked ذكر and blocked سماع.
terra: The wrongdoers will hear and see with startling clarity when they come to God, although today they are plainly astray; the future scene reverses present failed perception.
terra: God grants Abraham and his family an exalted truthful mention among later people, showing a blessed form of becoming remembered speech.

luna: When the Most Merciful's verses are recited to earlier prophets, they fall prostrate and weep; the ayah shows an audible reminder moving its hearers to response. | terra: When the Merciful's signs are recited, the prophets and chosen ones fall prostrate and weeping; reception of the report becomes humble action.

luna: In the garden they hear no لَغْوًا, only peace, directly matching 88:11's exclusion of لَاغِيَةً and the section's question of what sound replaces silence. | terra: Paradise contains no heard لَغْوًا, only سَلَامًا; it states both the excluded speech and the word that replaces it in the section's protected soundscape.
terra: The Quran is made easy in the Prophet's tongue so he can give good news and warn, supporting the section's account of ذكر as something voiced for others.
terra: The Quran is sent as a تَذْكِرَةً for one who fears, so the same surah that asks about Moses' report first defines revelation as fear-awakening reminder.
terra: Whether speech is voiced aloud or kept secret, God knows the secret and what is still more hidden, setting a divine boundary around “unheard” words.

luna: وَهَلْ أَتَىٰكَ حَدِيثُ مُوسَىٰ repeats the section's opening “has the report come to you?” and then unfolds Moses' story. | terra: وَهَلْ أَتَىٰكَ حَدِيثُ مُوسَىٰ is the same address and formula as 88:1, here opening a past story delivered to the Prophet.

luna: Moses is told to listen to what is being revealed, an explicit scene of a messenger receiving divine speech by hearing. | terra: Moses is chosen and told to listen to what is revealed, a direct instance of speech reaching its first addressee by revelation and audition.
luna: After telling Moses to listen to revelation in 20:13, God commands worship and prayer for His remembrance; this ayah's own contribution is to make received speech issue in remembrance.

luna: The Prophet is told, “We relate to you news of what has passed,” and is given a reminder, joining narrated report to remembrance as the section does. | terra: After Moses' story, God says He relates earlier news to the Prophet and has given him a ذكر, explicitly naming story-report and reminder as one revelatory task.
terra: The trumpet is blown and the criminals are gathered, supplying the announced setting for the lowered voices and following of the caller in 20:108.
terra: The gathered people whisper among themselves about how briefly they stayed, an adjacent low-voiced exchange that prepares the “only a whisper” soundscape of 20:108.

luna: At the resurrection, people follow the caller without deviation, their voices are humbled before the Most Merciful, and only a whisper is heard; this stages the fear-driven hush named in the section. | terra: This is the section's exact acoustic counterpart: on the summoning Day voices خَشَعَتْ before the Merciful and the hearer detects only a whisper, turning the bowed face of 88:2 into bowed sound.
terra: Immediately after the hush of 20:108, intercession itself is restricted to one permitted by the Merciful and acceptable in speech, defining the boundary on utterance.
terra: God says, “Our signs came to you and you forgot them”; أَتَتْكَ and نَسِيتَهَا reverse the section's opening reception and closing command to make the report remembered.
terra: People's reckoning has drawn near while they remain heedless and turn away, another way the coming Day is treated as imminent while its hearers fail to respond.

luna: A new reminder from their Lord reaches the people, yet they listen while playing and their hearts are distracted; it reverses the attentive reception sought by 88:21. | terra: Whenever a newly renewed reminder, ذِكْرٍ مِّن رَّبِّهِم مُّحْدَثٍ, comes, they listen while playing; the ayah fuses the ح د ث, س م ع, and ذ ك ر lines while exposing failed reception.
terra: The people admitted to bliss are guided to pure speech, ٱلطَّيِّبِ مِنَ ٱلْقَوْلِ, positively naming the kind of utterance that replaces لاغية.
terra: Believers are commanded to avoid false speech, a specific earthly prohibition on the kind of corrupt utterance excluded from the Garden.
terra: The travelers have ears “with which to hear,” yet the real blindness belongs to hearts; the ayah explicitly relocates meaningful hearing from organ to understanding.

luna: The successful believers turn away from اللغو, extending the section's concern with speech that has no place in a purified life. | terra: Believers turn away from ٱللَّغْوِ, practicing in earthly life the exclusion of vain speech that characterizes the Garden.

luna: After successive peoples reject their messengers, God says He made them أحاديث; they become the cautionary reports that a hearer may one day be. | terra: Each people rejects its arriving messenger and is then made أَحَادِيثَ; it exactly realizes the section's warning that a hearer of the report can become a cautionary report.

luna: The condemned are told “be despised therein and do not speak to Me”; this punitive silence contrasts with the garden's freedom from harmful speech. | terra: The people of the Fire are ordered to remain despised and not speak to God, a punitive eschatological silence distinct from both Paradise's pure speech and Judgment's general hush.
terra: On the Day, tongues, hands, and feet testify about what people did, showing that final testimony sounds even when defendants cannot control their own account.

luna: When called to God's and the Messenger's judgment, believers answer “we hear and obey”; this puts the section's obedience-sense of hearing into a concrete response. | terra: When called to God and His Messenger, believers say “We hear and we obey,” a direct formula for responsive rather than merely acoustic hearing.
terra: The Messenger bears his assigned duty, the audience bears its own, and his obligation is only clear conveyance, sharply separating report from response.
luna: The rejecters call the Qur'an ancient tales that someone wrote down and dictates morning and evening, a specific denial of the revelation-borne report the section describes.
terra: The regretful person says a companion led him away from the Reminder after it had come to him, directly joining arrival of the message to failed retention.
terra: Noah's people are drowned after denying the messengers and made a sign for humankind, a nonlexical instance of failed hearers becoming later warning.

luna: When the servants of the Merciful are addressed harshly by the ignorant, they answer with peace; it shows peace replacing an ugly exchange. | terra: When the ignorant address the Merciful's servants, they answer “peace”; an earthly encounter turns hostile or foolish speech into the very word heard in Paradise.

luna: The servants of the Merciful pass by laghw with dignity rather than joining it, an earthly counterpart to the garden's absence of such speech. | terra: The servants of the Merciful do not witness falsehood and pass by ٱللَّغْوِ with dignity, defining a present relation to the speech absent in Paradise.

luna: When reminded of their Lord's signs, the servants do not fall on them deaf and blind; it depicts receptive hearing rather than the refusal described elsewhere. | terra: The servants of the Merciful do not meet reminder of God's signs as if deaf and blind, defining remembrance as alert reception.
terra: The patient servants are rewarded with the high chamber and met there with greeting and peace, another Paradise scene filled with salutary speech.

luna: Whenever a new reminder comes from the Merciful, the rejecters turn away; the incoming word is present but refused, unlike the hearer who carries it onward. | terra: Every newly renewed reminder from the Merciful reaches them only for them to turn away, linking incoming speech, ذكر, and refusal to hear it responsively.
terra: The command to recite Abraham's news makes the messenger voice a past story for present hearers, paralleling the report openings gathered in the section.
terra: Abraham asks for a truthful tongue or honorable mention among later peoples, a positive reversal of condemned communities becoming cautionary reports.
terra: Revelation descends upon the Prophet's heart “so that you may be one of the warners”; the recipient of divine speech is thereby made its transmitter.
terra: The revelation comes in a clear Arabic tongue, supplying the linguistic form of the warning placed on the Prophet's heart in 26:194.
terra: No town is destroyed without warners having reached it, so becoming a ruined example follows a prior opportunity to hear.
terra: The warners serve as reminder and God does not wrong the town, explaining why delivered warning precedes the cautionary history of 26:208.

luna: The Prophet is told he cannot make the dead hear or make the deaf hear the call when they turn away; hearing here means receiving the reminder, beyond catching sound. | terra: The Prophet cannot make the dead or the retreating deaf hear the call, a direct boundary around his commission to speak the reminder.
terra: The Prophet can make only believers who submit hear, completing 27:80's limit with the identity of receptive listeners.

luna: The Qur'an recites to the Prophet news of Moses and Pharaoh in truth for people who believe, a clear example of a report about an earlier scene arriving by revelation. | terra: God recites to the Prophet some of the news of Moses and Pharaoh in truth for believing hearers, making old events present through revelation.

luna: Those given Scripture turn away when they hear اللغو and answer with peace; the passage links hearing to refusing empty or abusive talk. | terra: When believers hear ٱللَّغْوَ they turn away and answer with peace; their earthly discipline joins the section's two Paradise motifs, exclusion of vain speech and the hearing of salām.
terra: The Prophet cannot guide even whom he loves; God gives effective guidance, another boundary between speaking the reminder and producing its result.
terra: God does not destroy towns until a messenger in their center recites His signs to them; judged peoples first become hearers of warning.
terra: After peoples before them denied, the ayah says the Messenger's duty is only clear conveyance, linking the recurring rejection stories to his present role.
terra: At one call from God, people emerge from the earth, a concise counterpart to the Judgment procession following its caller.

luna: The same limit is stated again: the Prophet cannot make the dead or the deaf hear the call when they turn away, tying the reminder role to the hearer's response. | terra: The repeated statement that the Prophet cannot make the dead or retreating deaf hear defines nonresponse as beyond the speaker's control.
terra: After saying the Prophet cannot make the dead or deaf hear, the passage says he makes only believers who submit hear, defining effective hearing positively.

luna: Some people acquire لَهْوَ الْحَدِيثِ to divert others from God's path; this is speech used to distract, set against the section's report that calls its hearer to remembrance. | terra: لَهْوَ ٱلْحَدِيثِ is purchased to mislead people from God's way; this diverting discourse is the moral opposite of the truthful حديث meant to be heard and remembered.
terra: When God's signs are recited, the arrogant person turns away as though he had not heard and as though his ears were blocked, dramatizing hearing without reception.

luna: The section's lexicon extends laghw to noise and dog barking; this ayah calls the donkey's bray the most disagreeable sound, a plausible sound parallel though it names a different animal and not laghw. | terra: Lowering the voice is urged because the harshest voices are donkeys' voices; this is an analogical parallel to the dictionary's animal-noise branch of لغو, though the animal and root differ.
terra: Those who forgot the meeting of their Day are told that they are now forgotten, showing the consequence of letting warning fail to become remembrance.
luna: The Prophet's household is told to remember what is recited in their homes of God's signs and wisdom, joining recitation to remembrance as the section's definition does.
terra: The believers' greeting on the Day they meet God is سَلَامٌ, making peace the eschatological word of welcome.

luna: After the people of Saba' complain and are scattered, God says He made them أحاديث, directly illustrating the section's secondary sense of people turned into exemplary reports. | terra: After the people reject their provision and are scattered, God makes them أَحَادِيثَ, the precise dictionary branch in which destroyed people become exemplary tales.
terra: Good words ascend to God and righteous action raises them, giving morally sound speech a destination and weight unlike vain utterance.

luna: The Prophet is called only a warner and cannot make those in graves hear; the verse sets a limit on making the received warning take effect. | terra: God makes whom He wills hear, while the Prophet cannot make those in graves hear; the giver of effective hearing is distinguished from the human reminder.
luna: The Garden's inhabitants say praise to God for removing their grief; it gives another example of meaningful speech in place of futile talk.
terra: The people of Hell are reminded that they lived long enough for one who would remember and that a warner came, so belated pleading is answered by the report they ignored.
terra: Warning benefits the one who follows the reminder and fears the Merciful unseen, specifying the hearer whom prophetic speech can actually move.
terra: The town's messengers say their duty is only clear conveyance, the same stance voiced collectively inside a cautionary story.

luna: The garden's greeting is “Peace,” a word from a merciful Lord, giving a specific positive utterance where 88:11 says no ugly speech is heard. | terra: سَلَامٌ قَوْلًا مِّن رَّبٍّ رَّحِيمٍ makes peace a spoken word from the Merciful Himself within Paradise.

luna: On that Day mouths are sealed while hands and feet testify; it gives a punitive bodily silence distinct from the Garden's protected quiet. | terra: On that Day mouths are sealed while hands speak and feet testify; it reverses ordinary speech and shows that silencing human voices cannot silence the truth of their deeds.
terra: People in Paradise turn to one another asking questions, confirming from another Garden passage that absence of vain speech does not mean absence of meaningful conversation.

luna: The question هَلْ أَتَىٰكَ نَبَأُ الْخَصْمِ introduces the litigants climbing into David's chamber; its arrival-of-news formula opens a staged account like the section's question, using nabāʾ rather than hadith. | terra: وَهَلْ أَتَىٰكَ نَبَؤُا ٱلْخَصْمِ uses the same question and addressee as 88:1 with نبأ instead of حديث, then opens a narrated encounter.
terra: After accounts of earlier prophets, “this is a reminder” turns the just-narrated stories into present moral recollection for the audience.
terra: The Prophet is commanded to say, “It is tremendous news,” another direct designation of the warning proclamation as eschatological news.
terra: The audience turns away from the tremendous news named in 38:67, making failed reception rather than lack of delivery the problem.
terra: The proclamation is only a reminder to the worlds, giving the report the same outward movement implied when the first hearer becomes a reminder.

luna: The praised servants listen to speech and follow its best; the ayah shows سماع as understanding and choosing a response, not merely catching sound. | terra: The guided servants listen to “the word” and follow its best, a direct enactment of سماع as comprehension and obedience rather than bare audition.

luna: The Qur'an itself is called أَحْسَنَ الْحَدِيثِ; its repeated recitation moves reverent listeners from shivering to softened hearts and remembrance. | terra: God sends down “the best حديث”; skins shiver and then hearts soften to God's remembrance, joining revealed report, fearful bodily humility, and ذكر in one response.
terra: God sends the Book to the Prophet for humankind in truth, but the Prophet is not a trustee over those who choose error; received revelation and limited authority appear together.
terra: At Hell's gates the keepers ask whether messengers came reciting signs and warning of this very meeting; the future report has become the hearer's present scene.

luna: At the Garden's gates its keepers greet the entrants with peace; it adds a specific positive utterance to the section's account of what is heard there. | terra: At Paradise's opened gates its keepers say “Peace be upon you; you have done well; enter,” contrasting the received words at Hell's gates in 39:71.
luna: Once in the Garden, its people say praise to God for fulfilling His promise and giving them the Garden; the verse supplies meaningful praise within the scene of protected speech.
terra: The Prophet is commanded to warn of the approaching Day when hearts choke in throats, bringing the still-future scene near through present speech.
terra: Hell's keepers ask whether messengers came with clear proofs; the condemned admit they did, again measuring the realized scene against previously delivered warning.
terra: Some messengers' accounts are related to the Prophet and others are not, explicitly presenting prophetic history as selected revealed report.
terra: At the Fire, people's hearing, sight, and skins testify against them; the faculty that once received warning becomes a speaker in the final account.
terra: They ask their skins why they testified, and the skins answer that God made them speak; ordinary control of voice is reversed in the Judgment scene.

luna: The rejecters say not to listen to the Qur'an and to make laghw over it; their deliberate cacophony reverses the attentive, purified hearing of the section. | terra: Unbelievers command one another not to listen to the Quran and to make noise, وَٱلْغَوْا فِيهِ; earthly noise is used to block the revealed report that Paradise later excludes as لغو.
terra: The Quran is guidance and healing for believers but deafness to unbelievers, as though they are called from far away; one report becomes intelligible or inaudible according to reception.
terra: God is guardian over those who take other protectors, while the Prophet is not their trustee, preserving the same division between reminder and divine oversight.
terra: The condemned are shown humbled, خَاشِعِينَ مِنَ ٱلذُّلِّ, looking furtively at the Fire; it shares the Judgment posture behind the section's bowed faces and voices.

luna: When people turn away, the Prophet is told he was not sent as their keeper and has only to convey; it marks the boundary of the reminder's messenger, as 88:21-22 does. | terra: If they turn away, the Prophet was not sent as their guardian; upon him is only conveyance, closely restating both 88:21 and 88:22.
terra: The ayah identifies revelation, speech from behind a veil, and a sent messenger as God's modes of speaking to a human, grounding the section's definition of words arriving through revelation.
terra: God says He revealed a spirit from His command to the Prophet and made it light for guidance, applying the revelatory mode named in 42:51 to this messenger.
terra: The question whether the Prophet can make the deaf hear or guide the plainly astray reinforces that his task is delivery, not control of reception.
terra: Pharaoh's people are made a precedent and example for later peoples; without using أحاديث, it develops the same transformation of judged hearers into exemplary history.
terra: Those plotting are asked whether God does not hear their secrets and private counsel, while messengers record it; apparently unheard speech still enters the final record.
terra: The question “how can reminder benefit them?” is answered by the fact that a clear messenger already came and was rejected, making later recognition too late.
terra: God makes the revelation easy on the Prophet's tongue so that people may remember, directly tracing the section's movement from speech on a tongue to memory in listeners.

luna: After God's signs are recited, the ayah asks what حديث people will believe in after God and His signs, treating revelation as the decisive report. | terra: God's signs are recited in truth and the hearers are asked what حديث after God and His signs they will believe, defining the revealed report against rival speech.
terra: The sinner hears God's signs recited yet persists arrogantly as if he had not heard them, another exact boundary between sound reaching the ear and meaningful listening.
terra: God says the condemned are “forgotten” that Day as they forgot meeting it, an eschatological reversal of the reminder they failed to retain.
terra: The jinn listen to the Quran, command silence, and then return to warn their people; a first audience becomes the next bearer of the heard report.
terra: The returning jinn say they heard a revealed book confirming Moses and guiding to truth, giving the content they transmit after the listening scene of 46:29.
terra: They call their people to answer God's caller and believe, completing the section's movement from receiving a report to placing it in other ears.
terra: Some listen to the Prophet but leave asking what he just said; the heard sound fails to become understanding or retained reminder.
terra: The Hour can only come suddenly, yet its signs have already come; present evidence makes the future warning already operative.
terra: Believers must not raise their voices above the Prophet's or shout speech at him, making vocal restraint part of proper reception of the messenger.

luna: Those who lower their voices near God's Messenger have hearts tested for piety; this is reverent, deliberate lowering of sound, unlike the fear-hushed voices of the Judgment scene. | terra: Those who lower their voices before God's Messenger are praised for tested hearts, a voluntary earthly humility in sound beside the involuntary hush before the Merciful.
terra: No word is uttered without a watcher ready to record it; spoken words do not vanish but become part of the account that closes surah 88.
terra: “Enter it in peace” is the enduring Day's welcome, another wholesome utterance marking admission to Paradise.

luna: The account is called a reminder for whoever has a heart or gives ear while present, explicitly joining remembrance to attentive listening. | terra: The preceding ruined peoples are a reminder for one who has a heart or “casts the ear” attentively, making past news effective only through present receptive hearing.
terra: The addressee is commanded to listen for the Day when the caller calls from a near place, carrying the section's address to the final sound itself.
terra: On that Day people hear the Cry in truth and emerge, specifying what the commanded listening of 50:41 anticipates.

luna: The Prophet is told to remind by the Qur'an whoever fears God's threat, specifying the report used by the reminder in 88:21. | terra: The Prophet is not a compeller over them and must remind with the Quran whoever fears the warning, almost exactly combining 88:21's task with 88:22's limit.

luna: هَلْ أَتَىٰكَ حَدِيثُ ضَيْفِ إِبْرَاهِيمَ repeats the report-arrival formula and opens the account of Abraham's honored guests. | terra: هَلْ أَتَىٰكَ حَدِيثُ ضَيْفِ إِبْرَاهِيمَ opens Abraham's guest story with the same report-reaching-the-addressee formula.

luna: The command “remind, for the reminder benefits believers” states the purpose of the speech 88:21 assigns to the Prophet. | terra: The direct command وَذَكِّرْ says reminder benefits believers, closely matching the closing commission of 88:21.

luna: This garden scene excludes both idle and sin-inducing speech, another precise formulation of what 88:11's لا تسمع concerns. | terra: Paradise drinking produces neither لَغْوٌ nor sin-incurring talk, another direct formulation of an environment cleansed of corrupt speech.

luna: After 52:23 says the Garden has no idle or sinful speech, this ayah says its people turn to one another in conversation; its own contribution shows the silence excludes bad talk, not all speech. | terra: Immediately after the absence of لغو in 52:23, Paradise's people turn to one another and ask questions; their conversation shows that the promise removes corrupt speech rather than all speech.

luna: Following the conversation begun in 52:25 after 52:23's exclusion of laghw, the people say they had been apprehensive among their families; this gives the garden conversation a reflective, meaningful content.
terra: The Prophet is commanded to remind despite accusations of soothsaying or madness, preserving his speaking role amid hostile reception.
terra: Deniers are challenged to produce a حديث like the revelation if truthful, marking this heard discourse as inimitable rather than ordinary talk.
terra: The approaching event has drawn near and none but God can uncover it, another compact announcement of the future as already at hand.

luna: The listeners are challenged about this hadith and their response of laughter rather than tears, a specific example of hearing revelation without its intended response. | terra: The audience is asked whether it marvels at “this حديث,” identifying the recited warning itself as the report that now demands a humbled response.
terra: Immediately after being confronted with “this report” in 53:59, the hearers laugh rather than weep; their reaction reverses the humbled, tearful reception that the section's news calls for.
terra: The hearers remain heedlessly preoccupied after 53:59 confronts them with the report; the ayah contributes the inattentive stance between laughter and the command to prostrate.
terra: The passage about the audience's response to “this report” ends by commanding prostration and worship, supplying the bodily humility appropriate to what has been heard.
terra: The Hour has drawn near, making the future event grammatically immediate in the same direction as 88's already-arrived report.
luna: The surah says reports have come to the rejecters containing deterrence; the news is a warning whose audience may heed it or refuse it.
terra: The Prophet is told to turn from rejecters until the Day the caller summons them to something terrible, setting the call that draws the humbled eyes of 54:7.
terra: With eyes خُشَّعًا people emerge from graves and move toward the caller, joining bodily humility to the same summoned Judgment scene as the silenced voices of 20:108.
terra: People hasten toward the caller and unbelievers name it a hard Day, completing the summoned, humbled procession begun in 54:6–7.

luna: After Noah's people are warned, the refrain says the Qur'an was made easy for remembrance and asks who will remember; it ties a delivered warning to its hearer. | terra: After Noah's destruction, the Quran is said to be made easy for remembrance and asks whether anyone will remember, turning the narrated people into warning for a new hearer.

luna: The same refrain follows the warning to 'Ad, repeating the link between recited admonition and a hearer's remembering. | terra: After ʿĀd's fate, the repeated invitation to remember makes the old catastrophe a present test of reception.

luna: After Thamud's destruction, the same refrain makes the account itself an accessible reminder for its audience. | terra: After Thamud's fate, the same refrain offers the transmitted story as an accessible reminder before its hearer repeats it.

luna: After Lot's people are warned and punished, the refrain again asks who will remember the delivered account. | terra: After Lot's people, the final repeated refrain again joins a destroyed people's news to the audience's opportunity to remember.

luna: The garden dwellers hear neither idle speech nor sinful words, spelling out the kind of utterance absent from the soundscape of 88:11. | terra: The blessed hear neither لَغْوًا nor speech that incurs sin, precisely expanding the kind of word excluded by 88:11.

luna: The next ayah supplies the positive sound: only words of peace are heard, giving a fitting utterance in place of harmful talk. | terra: After 56:25 removes vain and sinful speech, this ayah supplies the audible remainder, “peace, peace,” so Paradise's silence is shown to be purification rather than muteness.
terra: The hearers are asked whether they treat “this حديث” lightly, exposing a dismissive response to the revealed report within a surah that also describes Paradise's purified hearing.
terra: After 56:81 asks why the audience treats “this report” lightly, this ayah identifies denial as their return for divine provision, making the hearer's response explicit.

luna: The ayah asks whether believers' hearts should humble themselves to God's remembrance and the truth sent down, meeting the section's khushūʿ and reminder threads. | terra: Believers are asked whether it is time for their hearts to become humble, تَخْشَعَ, to God's remembrance and revealed truth; heard reminder should produce inward khushūʿ.
terra: God has heard the woman disputing with the Prophet and complaining to Him, and He hears their dialogue; a human utterance reaches the divine Hearer and becomes revealed report.
terra: No private counsel escapes God's presence, and He will inform its speakers on Resurrection Day; speech unheard by other people still becomes final disclosure.
terra: Satan makes his party forget God's remembrance, naming the force by which a received reminder can be displaced.
terra: Those who forget God are made to forget themselves, extending the section's opposition between reminder and forgetting to loss of self-knowledge.
terra: If the Quran descended on a mountain it would be seen خَاشِعًا and split from fear, extending the section's humbled face and voice to creation's response to revelation.
terra: “Has the news not come to you” of earlier unbelievers is immediately followed by the evil consequence they tasted, making reception of old news a warning about the hearer's own future.
terra: If people turn away, the Messenger's duty is only clear conveyance, another exact boundary around transmitted speech.
terra: God declares that He has sent down a reminder to the audience, presenting ذكر itself as something that arrives from above.
terra: A messenger recites God's clear signs to bring believers from darkness to light, specifying the human voice through which the reminder of 65:10 reaches them.

terra: A private حديث passes from the Prophet to a wife, is disclosed, and is then made known to him by God; it concretely shows speech traveling by hearing and by revelation, with disclosure as its moral boundary.
terra: As people are thrown into Hell, its keepers ask whether a warner had come to them; their present fate is explicitly measured against earlier reception of warning.
terra: They confess that a warner did come but they denied him, supplying the rejected report whose failure to be heard leads to 67:10's regret.

luna: The people of the Fire regret that they did not listen or reason; the ayah makes failed hearing and understanding consequential, as the section's warning-report implies. | terra: People in the Fire say that had they truly listened or reasoned they would not be its inhabitants; سماع here plainly means receptive understanding, not sound alone.
terra: On the Day their eyes are humbled and abasement covers them, a close visual parallel to the faces خاشعة in 88:2 whose acoustic counterpart the prose develops.
terra: God tells the Prophet to leave to Him whoever denies “this حديث”; the revealed report is the Prophet's to deliver, while requital remains God's work.
terra: The Quran is only a reminder to the worlds, directly defining the “report” by its work in successive hearers.

luna: The ark's rescue is made a reminder, the ayah says, for an ear that retains it; it pictures the hearer holding a report as remembrance. | terra: God makes the saving event a تَذْكِرَةً and an attentive ear retains it; this is the section's whole passage from narrated news through hearing to awakened memory.
terra: The rejecters see the promised event as remote, giving the audience's temporal stance that the already-arrived form of the section's report corrects.
terra: God sees the promised event as near, reversing the distance assigned to it by the hearers in 70:6.
terra: They emerge rapidly with eyes humbled and humiliation covering them, another summoned-Day embodiment of khushūʿ.
terra: The Prophet is told by revelation that a group of jinn listened and said they had heard a wondrous Quran; hearing becomes both their testimony and fresh revealed news.
terra: The jinn say the Quran they heard guides to right conduct, so they believe in it; this states what happens when the heard revelation becomes understanding and obedience.
terra: The jinn say that when they heard the guidance they believed, a direct formula for سماع producing the receptive response the section distinguishes from bare audition.
terra: “This is a reminder” and whoever wills may take a way to his Lord; the heard warning opens a route but does not compel the hearer.
luna: The passage says the number of the Fire's guardians is a trial and reminder for believers and scripture readers; it shows a disturbing report serving admonition.

luna: The Qur'an is called a reminder, directly naming what the Prophet's فَذَكِّرْ in 88:21 carries. | terra: The warning text is itself a تَذْكِرَةٌ, identifying revelation by the work that 88:21 commissions the Prophet to perform.

luna: Whoever wills may take heed of that reminder; the ayah supplies the listener's side of 88:21's reminder exchange. | terra: Whoever wills may remember it, locating the response to the reminder of 74:54 in the hearer's own reception.
terra: The Prophet is told not to move his tongue hastily with the revelation, a precise glimpse of the first recipient preparing to voice what he receives.
terra: The Prophet is told that when God recites the revelation he should follow its recitation, showing the first messenger as a listener before he becomes its voice.

terra: هَلْ أَتَىٰ opens with the same interrogative arrival formula, but asks about a time that passed over humanity before it was a thing mentioned; it offers a formal and temporal counterpoint to news arriving to the Prophet.
terra: The repeated declaration that the revelation is a reminder leaves taking the way to God to the willing listener.

luna: The Day is described as one when people do not speak, a stark boundary beside 20:108's whisper and the Garden's speech free of laghw. | terra: “This is a day when they will not speak” gives an uncompromising Judgment silence parallel to the voices hushed in the section.
terra: They are not permitted to offer excuses, explaining the specific denied speech behind the silence stated in 77:35.

luna: After the warnings in the surah, the question فَبِأَيِّ حَدِيثٍ بَعْدَهُ يُؤْمِنُونَ makes the Qur'anic message itself the report whose hearing calls for belief. | terra: The warning surah ends by asking what حديث after it they will believe, placing responsibility on the audience that has just heard the coming Day narrated.

luna: The surah opens by asking about the great news, then identifies the disputed subject; it makes the coming judgment a report people are already discussing. | terra: The opening question “about what are they asking one another?” makes a heard dispute the doorway to the great resurrection-news named in 78:2.
terra: The disputed ٱلنَّبَإِ ٱلْعَظِيمِ is the coming resurrection, another future overwhelming event presented to present hearers as “the great news.”

luna: The garden has neither laghw nor falsehood to be heard, extending the section's protected silence from ugly speech to lying. | terra: In the Garden they hear neither لَغْوًا nor denial or lying; the second exclusion sharpens the section's gloss of لاغية as morally ugly speech.

luna: On the Day of the Spirit and angels standing in rows, none speaks except by the Merciful's permission and with a right word; it gives a boundary to the judgment-day hush. | terra: On the Day the Spirit and angels stand in ranks, none speaks except one permitted by the Merciful who says what is right; silence has a divinely bounded exception.

luna: Among the resurrection scene's trembling hearts, the eyes are described as humble; it repeats khashʿ in the same Day setting while applying it to eyes rather than voices. | terra: In the Day's terror, eyes are خَاشِعَةٌ; the visual humility parallels 88:2 while 20:108 supplies its silenced sound.

luna: هَلْ أَتَىٰكَ حَدِيثُ مُوسَىٰ uses the same “has Moses' report come to you?” opening as 88:1, then begins his story. | terra: هَلْ أَتَىٰكَ حَدِيثُ مُوسَىٰ repeats the section's question almost verbatim and again makes a past story arrive as heard revelation.
terra: On the Day the human will remember what he strove for, showing the final involuntary recollection toward which the present reminder points.

luna: The revelation is called a reminder, connecting the incoming report with the reminder the Prophet is then told to deliver. | terra: The revelation is called a تَذْكِرَةٌ, another direct description of the message as an awakening reminder.

luna: Whoever wills may remember it, showing the listener's choice in response to the reminder. | terra: Whoever wills may remember it, completing the movement from an offered reminder to memory in its recipient.
terra: The recitation is only a reminder to the worlds, another repeated formulation of the message passing beyond its first recipient.
terra: The transgressor answers recited signs with “tales of the ancients,” reversing the section's use of true past reports as revelation and reminder.
terra: When the Quran is recited to them they do not prostrate, reversing the humble embodied listening shown in 17:107–109 and 19:58.

luna: هَلْ أَتَىٰكَ حَدِيثُ الْجُنُودِ repeats the same report-arrival opening; 85:18 then identifies the armies with Pharaoh and Thamud. | terra: هَلْ أَتَىٰكَ حَدِيثُ ٱلْجُنُودِ opens the Pharaoh and Thamud recollection with the same formula, making ruined peoples into the report now heard.
terra: God promises to make the Prophet recite so that he will not forget, joining oral transmission with the memory required of the first recipient.

luna: “Remind, if the reminder benefits” closely parallels 88:21's command فَذَكِّرْ and its account of the Prophet as reminder-bearer. | terra: فَذَكِّرْ repeats 88:21's command to remind and makes the benefit of reminder the criterion for the prophetic address.
terra: The person who fears will remember, identifying the receptive hearer for the command in 87:9 and for the reminder in this section.
terra: When Hell is brought near, the human remembers, but the ayah asks what use that remembrance can then have; it is the too-late counterpart to the present command to remind.
